items.stem: Although the Supreme Court was the weakest of the three branches of government in the early days of the new republic, John Marshall strengthened the Court by
options: establishing the principle of federalism, giving federal courts the power to declare laws unconstitutional
declaring the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions, which asserted the right of states to nullify federal laws, unconstitutional
establishing the principle of judicial review in the case of McCulloch v. Maryland
establishing the principle of judicial review in the case of Marbury v. Madison
items.explanation: John Marshall was not the first chief justice of the Supreme Court, but he was responsible for giving the Court its teeth and much of the power it wields today. Marbury v. Madison was Marshall’s first significant decision and established the principle of judicial review, which enables the Court to declare a federal or state law unconstitutional. Choice (C), McCulloch v. Maryland, was another landmark decision of the Marshall Court. This decision dealt with the Second Bank of the United States and established the principle of federal supremacy.

option_explanations.A: Marshall did not establish 'federalism' — the division of power between nation and states predates him. The power to declare laws unconstitutional is judicial review, not federalism; this option mixes up the two concepts.
option_explanations.B: The Supreme Court never declared the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions (1798-99) unconstitutional. Those resolutions asserted a state right to nullify federal laws, but no Court case struck them down.
option_explanations.C: McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) was a landmark Marshall decision, but it established federal supremacy and implied powers in the fight over the Second Bank of the United States — not judicial review.
option_explanations.D: Marbury v. Madison (1803) was Marshall's first major decision and established judicial review: the Court's power to declare federal or state laws unconstitutional, which gave the judiciary its lasting strength.

items.stem: The Louisiana Purchase was an important factor in the development of U.S. trade because it
options: opened new markets among the western Indian nations
gave the country complete control of the Mississippi River
added numerous French factories in the Louisiana Territory to the U.S. economy
facilitated the immediate completion of the transcontinental railroad
items.explanation: The Louisiana Purchase grew out of the government’s efforts to purchase New Orleans from the French. President Jefferson wanted control of the city because it sits at the mouth of the Mississippi River, an essential trade route. Jefferson sent James Monroe to France to negotiate the sale. The French, desperate for cash and nearly as desperate to divest themselves of New World holdings, offered to sell the entire massive Louisiana Territory. The United States would control both banks of the Mississippi River, as well as a tremendous amount of western land. As a result, American traders could travel the length of the river unimpeded and trade subsequently boomed. Many of the incorrect answers to this question are anachronistic; the date of the purchase was too early for there to be “numerous French factories” in the territory, as in (C), or to allow for “the immediate completion of the transcontinental railroad,” as in (D).

option_explanations.A: New markets among western Indian nations were not the trade significance of the purchase. Jefferson wanted New Orleans and the Mississippi — the artery for American commerce.
option_explanations.B: The purchase gave the United States both banks of the Mississippi River plus New Orleans at its mouth, securing complete American control of the essential trade route to the Gulf.
option_explanations.C: French trading posts were not the point of the purchase. The value was the Mississippi, the port of New Orleans, and the vast western land — not French industrial assets.
option_explanations.D: The transcontinental railroad was not completed until 1869, more than six decades later. It belongs to a much later era and had nothing to do with the 1803 purchase.

items.stem: As a result of the Hartford Convention following the War of 1812,
options: the Federalist Party lost credibility and eventually died out
the Constitution was amended to limit the president to two terms in office
the New England states threatened to secede
Congress passed the War Powers Act, limiting future presidents from gaining too much power during wartime, as Madison had
items.explanation: The War of 1812 was very unpopular with New England Federalists who called the war “Mr. Madison’s War.” The economic policies of Jefferson and Madison disrupted trade, and as a result, were detrimental to New England merchants and shippers. Consequently, a group of New England Federalists met in Hartford, Connecticut, in 1814 to articulate a list of grievances against the Democratic-Republicans and their policies. While some men suggested secession, others suggested amending the Constitution to protect New England’s commercial interests against what they perceived to be a dangerous, growing threat from the agrarian, Republican South. Because the British were “defeated” in the War of 1812, what is often termed the Second War for Independence, the Federalists were seen as big babies and discredited. With the election of James Monroe in 1816, the United States had entered the Era of Good Feelings, a relatively brief period when there was only one political party—the Republicans. Although the War of 1812 damaged New England commerce initially, in the long run, the Embargo Act of 1807 and the War of 1812 forced Americans to be less dependent on British goods and indirectly stimulated the growth of industry in antebellum New England.

option_explanations.A: New England Federalists met at Hartford in 1814 to air grievances while the war was still on, which looked unpatriotic. When the war ended and Jackson triumphed at New Orleans, the party was discredited and soon disappeared.
option_explanations.B: No constitutional amendment limiting presidents to two terms came out of Hartford. The two-term limit remained custom until the 22nd Amendment in 1951.
option_explanations.C: Although a few delegates talked of secession, the convention itself issued grievances and proposed constitutional amendments — it did not threaten secession.
option_explanations.D: No War Powers Act was passed in this era; the War Powers Act dates to 1973. Madison's wartime power was not curtailed by any such law.

items.stem: Andrew Jackson accused Henry Clay of using his influence to broker the “corrupt bargain” of 1824 (which cost Andrew Jackson the election) because Clay
options: had been promised a cabinet post by John Quincy Adams
was promised the vice presidency if Jackson was defeated
knew Jackson did not support his “American System”
feared Jackson’s proslavery stance on states’ rights
items.explanation: The election of 1824 is one of the more infamous elections in American political history and exposes one of the unanticipated flaws in the Electoral College system. Because of the winner-take-all system of awarding electoral votes in most states, it is possible for a candidate to actually win the popular vote nationwide but lose the election. According to the Constitution, a candidate must win a majority, not a plurality, of electoral votes to win the presidential election. If no one candidate receives the requisite majority, the election is “thrown into the House,” and the House of Representatives chooses the president from among the top three candidates. In the event this occurs, each state casts only one vote. Because there were five candidates running for president in 1824, it was almost impossible for anyone to receive a majority. Realizing that he did not have enough support to win the presidency, Henry Clay threw his support to John Quincy Adams in exchange for Adams’s promise to make Clay his secretary of state. Jackson believed he lost the election because of this “corrupt bargain.”

option_explanations.A: With no candidate winning an Electoral College majority in 1824, the House chose among the top three, and Clay — as Speaker — threw his support to Adams. Adams then named Clay Secretary of State, which Jackson denounced as a 'corrupt bargain.'
option_explanations.B: Clay was not promised the vice presidency. John C. Calhoun became vice president under Adams; Clay's reward was the State Department.
option_explanations.C: Jackson's opposition to Clay's American System was real, but it was not the mechanism of the alleged bargain. The charge centered on Clay's House influence being traded for a cabinet post.
option_explanations.D: Fears about Jackson's position on slavery and states' rights were not the basis of the 'corrupt bargain' charge, which was about the House vote and the Secretary of State appointment.

items.stem: The controversy over the tariff during the late 1820s and early 1830s demonstrated that
options: New Englanders were more radical than Southerners, as they had been since the days of the American Revolution
Andrew Jackson favored states’ rights over federal supremacy
the system of checks and balances was flawed
economic sectionalism was a serious threat to national unity
items.explanation: The tariff in question here is the infamous Tariff of Abominations, so named by southern states which protested that this protective tariff benefited New England manufacturers at the expense of cotton exporters in the South. The enactment of the Tariff of 1828 led to the Nullification Crisis a few years later when South Carolina declared the tariff null and void. (A similar situation had occurred in 1798 when Jefferson and Madison penned the Virginia and Kentucky resolutions in protest against the Alien and Sedition Acts.) In the case of Marbury v. Madison , Marshall opined that only the Supreme Court, not individual states, could rule a law to be unconstitutional. Eventually, a compromise tariff was brokered, and the crisis was resolved. Nevertheless, the Nullification Crisis during Andrew Jackson’s administration exposed the increasing tension of economic sectionalism that would propel the nation to civil war 30 years later.

option_explanations.A: This reverses the actual alignment. The radicals in the tariff fight were Southerners — South Carolina nullified the tariff — while New England manufacturers benefited from the protection.
option_explanations.B: In the Nullification Crisis Jackson defended federal supremacy, not states' rights: he pushed the Force Bill through Congress and threatened military action against South Carolina.
option_explanations.C: The crisis did not expose a flaw in checks and balances. The constitutional system worked — the dispute was settled politically with the Compromise Tariff of 1833.
option_explanations.D: The Tariff of Abominations (1828) protected Northern manufacturers at the expense of Southern cotton exporters, and South Carolina's nullification response showed how economic sectionalism could threaten national unity.

items.stem: Andrew Jackson’s positions on the Second National Bank and the American System typified his
options: distrust of large national government programs
abhorrence of the spoils system
tendency to favor the interests of the Northeast
commitment to developing a national economy
items.explanation: Andrew Jackson generally sided with the states on the issue of states’ rights, preferring to limit the powers of the federal government to only those he perceived to be essential. He also favored his Western constituency to the power elite of the Northeast, whom he regarded with suspicion. Thus, Jackson vetoed the recharter of the Second National Bank, a large federal program championed by Northeastern bankers, and opposed federally funded internal improvements under Clay’s American System.

option_explanations.A: Jackson vetoed the recharter of the Second National Bank and opposed federally funded internal improvements. Both stances reflect his suspicion of large national programs and of the Northeastern elite behind them.
option_explanations.B: Jackson did not abhor the spoils system — he embraced it, defending 'rotation in office' as democratic reform when he replaced federal officeholders with his own supporters.
option_explanations.C: Jackson distrusted the Northeast's power elite; his political base was in the South and West. Favoring Northeastern interests is the opposite of his profile.
option_explanations.D: Building up a national economy through federal programs was Henry Clay's American System, which Jackson opposed — not Jackson's own program.

items.stem: The Cherokee of Georgia were forced off their land because
options: they refused to assimilate to the “American” way of life
gold was discovered on Cherokee land in Georgia
the Supreme Court refused to hear their cases
the Seminole tribe, their traditional enemy, conquered their territory
items.explanation: The Cherokee were considered part of the “Five Civilized Tribes” living in the South, having established a republic in the state of Georgia. Unfortunately, the discovery of gold within the Cherokee nation’s borders was the catalyst for the tribe’s forced relocation. Georgian citizens wanted to enforce the Indian Removal Act in order to have access to the territory. Although the Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Cherokees, President Andrew Jackson did not comply with the decision. States’ rights were an important issue during Jackson’s presidency, and he did not want to intervene on behalf of the Cherokee nation.

option_explanations.A: The Cherokee had assimilated to a remarkable degree — a written constitution, a republican government, a newspaper — as one of the 'Five Civilized Tribes.' Assimilation did not save them from removal.
option_explanations.B: Gold was discovered on Cherokee land in Georgia in 1828-29, and the resulting land rush created overwhelming pressure to seize Cherokee territory and enforce removal.
option_explanations.C: The Supreme Court did hear the Cherokees' cases and ruled in their favor, notably in Worcester v. Georgia (1832). President Jackson simply refused to enforce the decision.
option_explanations.D: The Seminole did not conquer Cherokee territory. The Seminole lived in Florida and fought their own separate war against removal; they were not the cause of Cherokee dispossession.

items.stem: Brook Farm in Massachusetts, the Oneida Community in upstate New York, and New Harmony in Indiana were similar in that they
options: were religious communities inspired by the Second Great Awakening
demonstrated the attraction of communism to many Americans
failed because they practiced political and social equality within their own communities
were utopian communities designed to ameliorate the effects of a growing commercial society
items.explanation: Brook Farm, the Oneida Community, and New Harmony were all utopian communities that arose during the antebellum period in response to what some people perceived to be the ill effects of a growing commercial society.

option_explanations.A: Not all three were religious products of the Second Great Awakening. Brook Farm was Transcendentalist and New Harmony was the secular Owenite experiment; only Oneida was a religious community in the usual sense.
option_explanations.B: Calling this the attraction of 'communism' is anachronistic — Marx had not yet written. These were utopian socialist experiments, and 'communism' mislabels what drew people to them.
option_explanations.C: They did not fail because they practiced equality. Their failures came from financial troubles and internal conflicts, not from the principle of equality itself.
option_explanations.D: Brook Farm, Oneida, and New Harmony were all antebellum utopian communities founded by reformers who wanted to escape the perceived selfishness and instability of the growing commercial society.

items.stem: Which of the following statements was NOT consistent with the foreign policy of the Monroe Doctrine?
options: The United States had authority to intervene in the affairs of other nations in the Western hemisphere.
The United States would not interfere in the affairs of European powers.
European nations were not permitted to trade with nations of the Western hemisphere without U.S. consent.
European nations should stay out of the affairs of the Western hemisphere.
items.explanation: The Monroe Doctrine aimed to establish a policy of mutual noninterference with European governments. While largely unenforceable by the United States, it established that the United States would stay out of European affairs if Europe stayed out of affairs of the Western Hemisphere. While trade and diplomacy would still occur between Europe and the Americas, this foreign policy would aid in keeping the United States out of European conflicts during the 19th century.

option_explanations.A: The Doctrine asserted a U.S. sphere of influence in the Western Hemisphere, positioning the United States as its protector — consistent with claiming authority over hemispheric affairs.
option_explanations.B: Non-interference in European affairs was one half of the Doctrine's bargain: the United States would stay out of Europe's quarrels if Europe stayed out of the Americas.
option_explanations.C: The Monroe Doctrine never restricted European trade with the Americas. It opposed new European colonization and intervention in American governments; commerce and diplomacy across the Atlantic continued.
option_explanations.D: Warning European powers to stay out of the affairs of the Western Hemisphere is the core of the Monroe Doctrine — fully consistent with it.

items.stem: The greatest economic consequence of the early nineteenth-century boom in canal-building was
options: the speed with which goods were brought to market
the opening of western markets to eastern agricultural goods
the rapid population increase in western New York state alongside the Erie Canal
the major challenge it presented to railroads in the shipping industry
items.explanation: Prior to the canal era, it was an expensive and slow process to bring goods from the western part of the United States to the cities of the East Coast. (Imagine riding a horse-drawn cart from Ohio to New York City!) With the construction of the canals, such as the Erie Canal, this process was made immeasurably easier by boat, resulting in a drastic reduction of both price and time to market. Choice (B) is a reversal; it resulted in the opening of eastern markets to western goods, so eliminate (B). While the population did expand rapidly alongside the Erie Canal, this wasn’t an economic consequence, so eliminate (C). Finally, it was the railroads that presented a challenge to the canals, eventually ending their short-lived dominance over U.S. shipping. Eliminate (D).

option_explanations.A: Before canals, moving goods from the interior to the East Coast by wagon was slow and enormously expensive. Canals like the Erie slashed freight costs and transit time, getting goods to market faster and cheaper than ever before.
option_explanations.B: This reverses the main flow. Canals opened eastern markets to western agricultural goods (while also carrying eastern manufactures west) — the great gain was the interior's access to the seaboard, not the other way around.
option_explanations.C: Western New York did grow rapidly along the Erie Canal, but that population boom was a demographic side effect, not the greatest economic consequence of canal-building.
option_explanations.D: Canals did not challenge railroads — it was the other way around. Railroads came later and eventually eclipsed the canals as the dominant freight carriers.

items.stem: All of the following are true of the temperance movement in the United States EXCEPT
options: it originated largely through the efforts of German and Irish immigrant women
it was inspired by The Second Great Awakening
its ultimate success through the enactment of the 18th Amendment was facilitated by the fact that women’s suffrage was imminent
it was predominantly led by the middle and upper classes
items.explanation: The American temperance movement was originated and led by protestant women of the middle and upper classes who were inspired by the religious fervor of the Second Great Awakening. Largely a female-driven movement, its culmination in the 18th Amendment occurred just as women were being granted the right to vote. However, German and Irish immigrants (both male and female), many of whom were Catholic, tended to oppose the temperance movement.

option_explanations.A: German and Irish immigrants, many of them Catholic, generally opposed temperance rather than leading it. The movement was founded and led by Protestant women of the middle and upper classes.
option_explanations.B: The temperance movement drew directly on the moral-reform energy of the Second Great Awakening, which mobilized Protestants against drinking as a social sin.
option_explanations.C: The 18th Amendment (1919) was ratified just as women's suffrage was about to be secured (19th Amendment, 1920), and the prospect of women voters helped carry prohibition over the finish line.
option_explanations.D: Temperance was predominantly a middle- and upper-class movement, led by respectable Protestant women — not a working-class or immigrant cause.
